extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, USPTO examiners, policymakers, and legal scholars working on patent eligibility (especially for AI)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claims to AI-related inventions (datasets, methods, models, applications) satisfy patent eligibility under the Alice framework and related case law and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption / abstract idea focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claims excessively preempt the idea — courts ask whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea because it would 'tie up' basic tools of science and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption analysis is central: even a technologically meritorious advance may be ineligible if it 'totally preempt[s]' an idea (mathematical formulas are a canonical example). Courts examine whether claims focus on a specific means/method that improves the relevant technology or instead on a result/effect that itself is the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for a 'specific means or method that improves the relevant technology' (Bandai)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be evaluated to see whether they focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology rather than being directed to a result or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'specific asserted improvement' weighs against finding an abstract idea. The specificity of the improvement reduces preemptive effect; mere broad result-based claims are suspect. Courts treat specificity as evidence that the claim is technological rather than abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP intermediate prong: integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding a judicial exception, consider whether 'the claim recite[s] additional elements that integrate the [abstract idea] into a practical application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration exists when an improvement to computers or other technology is 'apparent' from the specification and the claims also disclose the improvement. If integration into a practical application is present, the claim is eligible and need not proceed to Alice step two. Examiners should look beyond the abstract idea to other claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of technological-improvement inquiry (step one vs step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and the Office may search for technological improvements at either Alice step one, step two, or both; the inquiry's purpose is to identify claim limitations that alleviate preemption concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether framed as 'technological improvements' (step one) or 'technological solution[s] to technical problem[s]' (step two), the same underlying search for features that prevent preemption is required. Dividing step one into an abstract-idea search and a specific-improvement search is one permissible approach, but attention to specificity and preemption should remain central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of the asserted improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts usually discuss a 'specific asserted improvement,' not just an improvement; specificity matters because it reduces preemption concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The degree of specificity and degree of improvement pull in opposite directions. Conclusory assertions of improvement do not suffice. Examiners and courts should require non-conclusory, concrete disclosure of how the claimed elements effect a specific technical improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of abstract ideas (MPEP: 3 categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP groups abstract ideas into three categories: '[m]athematical concepts,' '[c]ertain methods of organizing human activity,' and '[m]ental processes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP cautions examiners against finding abstract ideas outside these categories except in 'rare circumstances.' However, courts have not limited abstract ideas to only these categories, so examiners should not treat the list as exhaustive for judicial purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against tentative abstract-idea findings (examiner approval required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are strongly cautioned against finding an abstract idea that falls outside the core categories; tentative abstract-idea findings should be rare and require supervisory approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §2106.04(a)(3) requires approval of a superior for such rejections, meaning examiners should be conservative before asserting novel categories of abstract ideas. This is procedural guidance intended to limit overbroad abstract-idea rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify recited mathematical relationships or mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: At Alice step one, determine whether the claim recites mathematical relationships/formulas or a mental process (which would indicate a judicial exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must look to both claim language and the specification—for example, 'transformations' described as 'mathematical transformation functions' or 'training' described as gradient-based optimization are mathematical and can indicate an abstract idea even if a formula is not explicitly recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being 'deceived by the draftsman's art'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that disguise mathematical computation or abstract ideas with different terminology cannot avoid the abstract-idea inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to the substance: if the specification or claims disclose mathematical operations, data manipulation, or mentally performable steps, the abstract-idea exception can apply despite non-technical wording. Do not require explicit formulas to find a mathematical concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gathering and analyzing information of a specified content is a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that amount to 'gathering and analyzing information of a specified content' (e.g., collecting facial images and analyzing them) suggest an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims—especially when they do not invent the data, mathematical transformations, or neural networks themselves—are likely to be directed to an abstract idea. Courts treat routine data collection and analysis as basic tools that should not be monopolized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection alone is not usually a technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Data collection steps, by themselves, are unlikely to constitute a technological improvement sufficient to render an otherwise abstract claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data collection is the only thing beyond the abstract idea, allowing eligibility would permit evasion of Alice via trivial data-collection steps. Courts have warned that minimal narrowing by adding trivial data steps does not satisfy Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-concept analysis (Alice step two): elements other than the abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, determine whether the claim includes elements 'other than the judicial exception' that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., supply an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether non-exception elements constitute a technical solution to a technical problem and whether those elements meaningfully limit preemption. An inventive concept that merely appends conventional or routine steps will fail. Courts balance whether the claimed additional elements prevent monopolization of the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh technological solution against preemption risk at step two
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim discloses a technical solution (e.g., iterative training reducing false positives), evaluate whether allowing the claim would totally preempt the underlying idea (e.g., iterative training for facial recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim's non-abstract elements themselves would preempt basic tools or broadly claim the idea, the inventive-concept inquiry should weigh against eligibility. Look to whether remaining claim elements are substantive and limiting rather than generic or result-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-based claims and principles are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to results, effects, or principles (even innovative ones) are not patentable; a principle is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that claim a desired outcome rather than a specific technical means to achieve it are vulnerable. Courts have repeatedly held that claiming a result (even an innovative result) without more is an ineligible abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the invention gives computers new capabilities (Bandai/Enfish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'give computers new capabilities' or disclose a technological solution to a technological problem weigh against finding an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where software or AI provides an improvement in computer functioning (e.g., enabling a computer to perform previously human-only tasks), courts have been more likely to find eligibility. The claimed improvement should be specific and concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize AI inventions: dataset, method, model, application
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing AI-related claims, classify the asserted invention as a dataset, a machine-learning method, a trained model, or an application of a model—each category may merit different eligibility treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may include multiple categories; evaluation should focus on what the applicant asserts is inventive. Different policy and legal considerations apply to each category (see subsequent criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Datasets should generally be patent ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets (collections of data for training) are poor candidates for patent protection because they are redundantly protectable (trade secret, copyright), are unlikely to need patent incentives, and risk preempting broad scientific and economic activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dataset patents could chill routine data-collection and analysis; datasets are often not processes or compositions of matter under §101 and may be obvious. Courts should be skeptical of dataset claims on eligibility and obviousness grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of existing AI should generally be patent ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely apply existing AI technology to a new context (an 'application') should be treated as abstract ideas and denied patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such applications often require little inventive effort (low costs to conceive) and risk chilling downstream improvements that adapt models to contexts. Because applications often do not need patent incentives and can block subsequent improvements, they are poor candidates for patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods and trained models should usually be patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine-learning methods (how to train) and trained models (the programs that perform learned tasks) have stronger justifications for patenting because patents can incentivize their development without unduly chilling other innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When methods or models provide specific technical improvements to computers or technical processes, they are likely to satisfy the eligibility inquiry. Evaluation should still test for preemption, specificity, and whether claimed elements are more than conventional steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive assertions of improvement are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's bare assertion that a claim provides an improvement is not enough; the improvement must be supported and apparent from the specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts should require concrete disclosure of how claimed elements effect the asserted technical improvement. Mere conclusory language should be treated skeptically in both step-one and step-two inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-oriented eligibility consideration: innovation incentives, novelty, obviousness, utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis should be informed by patent-law goals—promoting innovation—alongside statutory requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, utility); whether patents will promote or hinder innovation should inform doctrinal application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether granting patents to the claimed subject matter will meaningfully incentivize the kind of inventive work required and whether it will unduly preempt future innovation. Consider redundancy with other IP regimes and the administrative role of the USPTO versus courts and Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedural safeguards for eligibility rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPEP instructs procedural limits on examiner actions: e.g., tentative abstract-idea findings outside core categories require supervisory approval, and certain other actions (egregious delays) also trigger director approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural rules are meant to limit overbroad or novel abstract-idea rejections and to ensure that unusual eligibility decisions receive higher-level review before issuance.
